summary: The letter pivots on one word: 'therefore.' Paul, the prisoner, begs them to walk worthily of the calling — with lowliness, patience, and eagerness to keep the unity of the Spirit. Seven unities are named: one body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God. Christ ascended and gave gifts — apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds, teachers — to build the body until it grows up into him. Then the walk turns specific: no longer as the Gentiles walk, in futility and callousness — put away the old man, be renewed, put on the new; so put away falsehood, be angry without sinning, steal no more but labor to give, speak what builds up, do not grieve the Spirit, put away bitterness, and forgive as God in Christ forgave you.
whyItMatters: This chapter is where the letter's first half becomes a way of life: the unity God made in Christ (2:14-16) must now be kept (4:3), the grace that saved (2:8) now walks (4:1), and the new humanity shows up in speech, work, anger, and forgiveness. The letter's ethics are never invented here — they are the calling worked out.

context.author: Paul, 'the prisoner in the Lord' (4:1) — the same chains as 3:1, now attached to a beg: the apostle pleads rather than commands.
context.audience: The whole assembly — the 'each one' who received grace (4:7), the body being built (4:12), the community whose words, work, and anger the chapter addresses household by household.
context.date: Undated; the chapter's horizon is growth — 'until we all attain' (4:13) — a process rather than a calendar.
context.setting: The practical half opens on the congregation's real life: gifted people, tired people, people who speak and steal and get angry — the unity of the Spirit lived where it can be tested.
context.literaryForm: Exhortation: a beg (4:1-3), a creed-like unities confession (4:4-6), a psalm quoted and explained (4:8-10), then imperatives stacked to the chapter's end.

outline.heading: Walk worthily of the calling
outline.note: The prisoner begs: walk worthily — lowliness, humility, patience, bearing one another in love, eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace; one body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, over all and through all and in us all.

outline.heading: The ascended giver and his gifts
outline.note: To each one grace was given; 'he ascended on high, he led captivity captive, and gave gifts to people' — the descended one is the ascended one who fills all things; the gifts are people — apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds, teachers — for perfecting the saints, the work of serving, the building up of the body, until the unity of the faith and the full grown measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ.

outline.heading: No longer children tossed by wind
outline.note: No longer infants, carried about by every wind of doctrine, by trickery — but speaking truth in love, growing up into him who is the head, Christ, from whom the whole body, fitted and knit together, makes itself increase in love.

outline.heading: The old walk put off
outline.note: No longer walk as the Gentiles walk — darkened, callous, given over to uncleanness; that is not the Christ they learned; put away the old man corrupting with deceit's lusts, be renewed in the spirit of the mind, and put on the new man created in righteousness and holiness of truth.

outline.heading: The new walk itemized
outline.note: Put away falsehood, speak truth — members of one another; be angry and do not sin, sun not going down on wrath, no place for the devil; steal no more — labor to share; no corrupt speech but what builds up and gives grace; do not grieve the Spirit of sealing; put away bitterness, wrath, anger, outcry, slander, malice — be kind, tender hearted, forgiving, as God in Christ forgave you.

keyVerses.text: I therefore, the prisoner in the Lord, beg you to walk worthily of the calling with which you were called, with all lowliness and humility, with patience, bearing with one another in love,
keyVerses.why: The hinge of the whole letter: 'therefore' — everything chapters 1–3 said God did now becomes a walk; and the walk's first equipment is not achievement but lowliness and patience.

keyVerses.text: There is one body and one Spirit, even as you also were called in one hope of your calling, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in us all.
keyVerses.why: The letter's unities confessed in one breath — seven 'ones' — the basis for being 'eager to keep the unity of the Spirit': the unity is made, not manufactured; the eagerness keeps what exists.

keyVerses.text: And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you.
keyVerses.why: The chapter's last word returns to the letter's foundation: forgiveness flowing downhill — the forgiven forgive. The new walk is not a new moral program but the calling answered in kind.

themes: keeping a unity that already exists

questions.question: What does the 'therefore' at 4:1 connect?
questions.answer: Everything: the calling is the one chapter 1 blessed — chosen, adopted, redeemed, sealed — and the seating of chapter 2, and the mystery of chapter 3. 'Walk worthily of the calling' means the walk answers what God did; the letter's ethics are never independent rules but the fitting response to its first half. Reading 4–6 without 1–3 is the most common way to lose this chapter's point.

questions.question: Why 'eager to keep the unity of the Spirit' — is unity made or kept?
questions.answer: Both, in the letter's order: Christ 'made both one' (2:14) — the unity exists as God's act — and the assembly is told to keep it, 'in the bond of peace' (4:3). The unities list that follows (one body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God) is not a goal to reach but a reality to guard. Human effort maintains what divine act created.

questions.question: What does 'he led captivity captive' mean?
questions.answer: Paul quotes Psalm 68 — a triumph song of God ascending as a victorious king, taking captives and receiving gifts — and applies it to Christ: the ascended one gives gifts to his people (4:8). The verse's force is the direction of movement — Christ descended first ('the lower parts of the earth,' 4:9, a phrase readers interpret as the grave, the incarnation, or both), then ascended 'that he might fill all things.'

questions.question: Who are the 'gifts' Christ gave the assembly?
questions.answer: People, not abilities: 'he gave some to be apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, shepherds and teachers' (4:11). Their purpose is stated exactly: 'for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ' (4:12) — the leaders equip; the saints do the work of service. A congregation where the gifts do everything and the saints do nothing inverts the sentence.

questions.question: How long is the gifts' work supposed to last?
questions.answer: 'Until we all attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to a full grown man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ' (4:13). The gifts are for growing up: the alternative to maturity is being 'children, tossed back and forth and carried about with every wind of doctrine' (4:14). The chapter gives no end date for the work — its measure is stature, not years.

questions.question: What is the 'old man' and the 'new man' in verses 22-24?
questions.answer: The chapter's anthropology in three moves: put away the old man — the former way of life 'that grows corrupt after the lusts of deceit'; be renewed in the spirit of the mind; put on the new man 'created in righteousness and holiness of truth' (4:22-24). The language of taking off and putting on clothes pictures conversion as a change of garment — and echoes the letter's earlier one-new-humanity claim (2:15): the new man is corporate as well as personal.

questions.question: 'Be angry, and don't sin' — is anger allowed?
questions.answer: The line quotes Psalm 4:4 and turns it into a rule with a time limit: anger is neither commanded nor forbidden here — it is fenced. 'Don't let the sun go down on your wrath, don't give place to the devil' (4:26-27). The instruction assumes anger happens and gives it a sunset clause: an anger that lodges becomes a place, and the place is the devil's.

questions.question: Why does the thief's instruction end with giving?
questions.answer: 'Let him who stole steal no more; but rather let him labor, producing with his hands something that is good, that he may have something to give to him who has need' (4:28). The chapter does not stop at don't: the replaced life is not mere honesty but generosity — work that ends in sharing. The walk is defined as much by its new direction as by what it left.

questions.question: What does it mean to 'grieve the Holy Spirit'?
questions.answer: The Spirit is personal — he can be grieved; and the chapter locates the grief in what follows: corrupt speech, bitterness, wrath, anger, outcry, slander, malice (4:29-31). The one 'in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption' (4:30) is treated as a resident, not a force: the community's words and tempers are the place he lives, and the chapter says its treatment of each other reaches him.

glossary.term: keep the unity of the Spirit
glossary.def: Guard the oneness God made (2:14) in the bond of peace (4:3) — human eagerness maintaining a divine fact.
The former self 'growing corrupt after the lusts of deceit,' put away, and the new self 'created in righteousness and holiness of truth,' put on (4:22-24).
The gifts' purpose (4:12): equipping God's people for the work of service — leaders outfit the saints, the saints do the ministry.
